name: The Osage Orange of Marcus Garvey Park

location.address: Southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park, Harlem, Manhattan

story:
This trunk does not rise so much as wrap around itself. The Osage orange in the southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park twists as it climbs, and in October 2024 that trunk earned it a place among New York City's Great Trees, when NYC Parks updated the list for the first time in about forty years.

The numbers back the shape. The trunk measures 58 inches across, more than four and a half metres round, and the Parks forestry inventory logged it again in May 2026 in good condition. That is a big tree for a species that grew up on the southern plains and was planted across the east mostly as a hedge.

It has also had a career in art. The Parks listing notes that the trunk features in Tree Reflections, a public piece by the artist Susan Stair that was shown at Conference House Park on Staten Island, at the far opposite end of the city.

Around it, the park keeps the name it took in 1973, after Marcus Garvey, having been Mount Morris Park before that. No planting date or age is on record for this Osage orange. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 58 inches across and twisting around itself as it climbs. It stands in the southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park.

name: The American Elm of Mapes Park

location.address: Mapes Park, near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue, Bronx

story:
When the city came to rebuild Mapes Park, the neighbours made sure the elm stayed. NYC Parks credits community members with working to protect this American elm during the park's renovation, and in 2024 it was named one of New York City's Great Trees.

The tree they stood up for is not a modest one. Its trunk measures 62 inches across, close to five metres round, and the Parks forestry inventory listed it in good condition in February 2026. No other elm in the park comes near it. Dutch elm disease spent the last century killing American elms across the continent, so a Bronx elm this broad is a survivor before it is anything else.

Mapes Park was one of the city's Community Parks Initiative projects, a programme for parks in neighbourhoods that had waited a long time for investment, and its ballfield was rebuilt in 2021. The elm came out of that period with a place on an official register.

It stands not far from the Bronx Zoo and the Botanical Garden, and a good deal quieter. How old the elm is has never been recorded, and nobody has published a planting date. If you know its history, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 62 inches across; no other elm in the park comes close. It stands in Mapes Park near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue.

name: The Sycamore of Morningside Park

location.address: Morningside Park, beside a path fork just north of the West 120th Street entrance, Manhattan

story:
Every London plane on a New York sidewalk is half this tree. The plane that lines the city's streets is a hybrid, and one of its parents is the American sycamore, the native species standing here in Morningside Park, in its pure form.

This one was named a Great Tree by NYC Parks in October 2024. Its trunk measures 48 inches across, nearly four metres round, and it stands beside a fork in the path just north of the West 120th Street entrance. In the Parks forestry inventory it is the only American sycamore of any real size in the whole park, so here the parent species stands among its hybrid descendants.

Morningside Park itself is a long strip of steep rock between Harlem below and Morningside Heights above, with the paths doing most of the climbing.

The forestry record for the tree dates from 2017, so the 2024 designation is the most recent official word that it stands. Nobody has published its age or a planting date. If you know how long it has been here, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only big American sycamore among the park's London planes, its trunk 48 inches across. It stands beside a path fork just north of the West 120th Street entrance.

name: The Weeping Willow of the Creative Little Garden

location.address: Creative Little Garden, 530 East 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan

story:
A weeping willow more than six storeys tall grows on the footprint of a tenement that burned. After a fire in the 1970s the city cleared the building at 530 East 6th Street and set the empty lot aside for gardening, and the Creative Little Garden opened there in 1978, run by volunteers from the first day.

The NYC Parks listing says the willow went in that same year, planted on the abandoned lot as a community effort. In 2024 Parks named it one of the city's Great Trees. A local report from that December gave its canopy as about 40 feet wide, hanging over a blue stone patio.

The measurements do not quite agree. The 2024 listing gives a trunk 37 inches across, while the Parks forestry inventory, updated in July 2026, records 42 inches and rates the tree only fair. Willows grow fast, and the same listing says this one lost a major branch some years ago, so read both figures as snapshots of a tree that keeps changing.

It is a garden tree, not a park tree. The gate opens only at the hours the volunteers post, so check before you go. Another Great Tree willow stands about 450 metres east in El Jardin del Paraiso, which makes the two an easy pairing on one walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the weeping willow hanging over the blue stone patio, more than six storeys tall. It stands inside the Creative Little Garden at 530 East 6th Street.

name: The Dawn Redwood of the Liz Christy Garden

location.address: Liz Christy Community Garden, Bowery and East Houston Street, Manhattan

story:
The woman who planted this tree in 1981 dug down until her shovel scraped the roof of the subway tunnel. Tessa Huxley put the dawn redwood into the Liz Christy Community Garden at the corner of the Bowery and Houston Street. A 2024 local report puts it at about 100 feet tall, visible along Houston Street all the way from Avenue B to Greene Street.

That is quick work for a species the world thought was extinct until the 1940s. Dawn redwoods were known from fossils before living trees were found in China, and seed from that find spread to gardens worldwide. This one went from sapling to skyline marker in roughly 45 years, which is the age its documented planting date gives it.

The garden is older still. Liz Christy and her neighbours began turning this vacant lot into a garden in 1973, and it is widely described as the city's first community garden. The same report says the air under the redwood is noticeably cooler than the street outside. NYC Parks lists it among the Great Trees of New York City.

Only that one report gives the height, so read the 100 feet as an estimate rather than a survey. The garden opens at posted volunteer hours, but the crown is easy to see from the street.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall conifer rising above the garden, the only dawn redwood on this corner. It stands inside the Liz Christy Community Garden at Bowery and East Houston Street.

name: The White Ash of Van Cortlandt Park

location.address: East side of the entrance to the cross-country trail, Van Cortlandt Park, Bronx

story:
This ash has a copy of itself across the park. A cloned sapling of the tree grows at the south end of the Parade Ground, and the original, one of the city's first official Great Trees, is still standing to compare it with.

That is no small thing for a white ash in North America. The emerald ash borer, a beetle that arrived from Asia in the early 2000s, has killed ash trees by the hundreds of millions, and big old ones have become rare. This one made NYC Parks' first Great Trees list in 1985, measured then at about 83 feet tall with a trunk 56.6 inches across. The current Parks figure is about 60 inches, close to five metres round. The forestry inventory looked at it in May 2026 and rated it fair, which for an ash of this size is a result worth reporting.

It stands on the east side of the entrance to the park's cross-country trail, where runners head off into the woods. The red horse chestnut by Van Cortlandt House is in the same park, an easy pairing.

The 1985 figures come to us through a transcription of the Parks entry rather than the page itself, and nobody has published an age for the tree. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 60 inches across, far bigger than the other ash nearby. It stands on the east side of the cross-country trail entrance; the young clone on the Parade Ground is a different tree.

name: The American Elm of Crotona Park

location.address: Crotona Park, near the Claremont Parkway entrance on Crotona Park East, Bronx

story:
The city counts Crotona Park's trees one by one, and in that inventory just one American elm has a trunk wider than 50 inches. This is that elm, 52 inches across and a little over four metres round, and in 2024 NYC Parks made it one of the Great Trees of New York City.

American elms once lined streets and greens across the Northeast. Dutch elm disease took most of them in the twentieth century, so a trunk this broad in a Bronx park is the exception. The Parks forestry inventory checked this one in July 2026 and rated it fair, so it is alive and being watched.

The Parks listing puts it on the north side of the park, near the entrance where Claremont Parkway meets Crotona Park East. The pin is close rather than exact, so look for the biggest elm near that entrance.

No source gives its height or its age, and nobody has published when it was planted. If you know its story, or have stood under it and measured it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the broadest American elm in the park, its trunk 52 inches across. It stands on the north side near the Claremont Parkway entrance on Crotona Park East.

location.address: El Jardin del Paraiso community garden, East 5th Street, Lower East Side, Manhattan

This willow is a classroom. Students from the New School have held a community gardening class in El Jardin del Paraiso since 2011, and the children of the nearby New Amsterdam School know the tree well too. It grows in what a 2024 local report calls the largest community garden on the Lower East Side, and that same year NYC Parks named it one of the Great Trees of New York City.

One story about its origin is too good to pass over and too thin to rely on. The same report says Liz Christy, whose name the garden on Houston Street carries, planted it here years ago. It gives no date, and no second source says so, so take it as a garden tradition rather than a fact.

What can be measured has been. The Parks forestry inventory holds a willow here with a trunk 41 inches across, a little over three metres round, rated fair in April 2025. Nobody has recorded which willow species it is, or how old.

The pin is close rather than exact, so look for the big willow inside the garden fence. The garden opens at hours its members post. The Great Tree willow of the Creative Little Garden stands about 450 metres west, an easy second stop. If you know when this one went in, or what kind of willow it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big willow inside the garden, its trunk 41 inches across. It stands in El Jardin del Paraiso on East 5th Street.

name: The Elms of the Heather Garden Promenade

location.address: Stan Michels Promenade above the Heather Garden, Fort Tryon Park, Manhattan

story:
Every other year, the elms of Fort Tryon Park get a vaccination. The Fort Tryon Park Trust pays to inoculate 48 American elms in the park against Dutch elm disease, the fungus that wiped out most of the species across the continent, and the two biggest American elms in the whole park stand along the Stan Michels Promenade.

The Trust describes the park's elms as more than a hundred years old, planted widely in the early 1900s, and says many of the originals have already been lost. The ones still standing line the promenade above the Heather Garden, which the Trust dates to 1935. The tree people talk about most is the large elm at the northern end of the promenade, whose low branches reach out over the garden beds.

Two trunks here stand out in the Parks forestry inventory, about 70 metres apart along the walk. The larger is 59 inches across, close to four and three quarter metres round. The other is 54 inches. Both were rated in good condition, the larger as recently as September 2026. No source says which of the two is the northern-end elm, so this entry covers the pair, and the pin sits on one of them.

The hundred years is the Trust's figure for the park's elms as a group, not a date for either tree. If you know more about these two, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two biggest elms along the promenade, about 70 metres apart, the larger 59 inches across. They stand on the Stan Michels Promenade above the Heather Garden.

name: The Ginkgo of the Cloisters Lawn

location.address: South end of the Cloisters Lawn, Fort Tryon Park, Manhattan

story:
A tree from a lineage older than the dinosaurs keeps watch over a lawn outside a museum of medieval Europe. The ginkgo at the south end of the Cloisters Lawn is one of NYC Parks' Great Trees of New York City, and it shares the hilltop at the north end of Fort Tryon Park with The Cloisters, the Metropolitan Museum's home for medieval art.

The Parks listing gives its trunk as 48 inches across. The forestry inventory, which rated it in good condition in February 2025, now records 52 inches, a little over four metres round. A gap of four inches between two measurements is normal growth or a tape held at a slightly different height, and either way this is a heavy ginkgo for a city tree.

There is a second large ginkgo in the park, about 450 metres south near the Heather Garden, so the lawn is the place to look. The pin sits on the big ginkgo nearest the lawn and is marked approximate until someone confirms it is the listed tree.

Nobody has published when it was planted. Ginkgos turn a clear butter yellow in autumn and tend to drop their leaves within a few days of each other, which makes late autumn the time to come. The lawn is public park and free; only the museum charges. If you know this tree's age, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves and a trunk about 52 inches across, the big ginkgo nearest the lawn. It stands at the south end of the Cloisters Lawn in Fort Tryon Park.

name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Weeping Beech Park

location.address: Margaret I. Carman Green (Weeping Beech Park), 37th Ave, Flushing

story:
This cedar is wider than it is tall. NYC Parks measured its crown at 59 feet across, and its trunk at 59 inches in diameter, close to four and three quarter metres round, on a tree only about 42 feet high. A cedar of Lebanon that grows out rather than up is doing exactly what the species does when it has room.

Its ground has a gardening pedigree. Parks says the tree began life in the nursery of Samuel B. Parsons, whose grounds ran through this part of Flushing, the same Parsons family whose weeping beech gave the little park its name. The famous beech died in 1998. The cedar is still here.

It was among the first trees NYC Parks named as Great Trees of New York City, in 1985, and it stayed on the list when the city renewed it in 2024. The trunk measurement on the register dates from that first nomination.

Nobody has published a planting date, and the nursery link does not give one. If you know when it went in, tell us. The weeping beeches of the park are about 50 metres away, which makes this a two-tree stop.

name: The Ginkgo of John Golden Park

How the tree and the fugitive are connected the Parks note does not spell out, and no second source backs it up, so treat it as local tradition with an official stamp rather than settled history. Tweed's escape itself is well documented. The tree's part in it is not.

name: The Fused Basswood of Fort Totten

location.address: Fort Totten Park, Underhill Rd and Officers Dr, Bayside

story:
Several trunks grew into one here. This American basswood started out with multiple trunks, and long ago they fused together, so that NYC Parks now measures the combined trunk at 99 inches across, close to 100. That is a figure for a merged mass of stems rather than a single trunk, and it is why the tree looks far wider than a single basswood trunk would be.

Parks named it one of the Great Trees of New York City in 2024. It stands at the corner of Underhill Road and Officers Drive inside Fort Totten Park, the former army post at the mouth of Little Neck Bay, whose grounds are now open to walkers.

Basswood, which Europeans would call a lime or linden, is a native of these woods, with large heart-shaped leaves and, in early summer, small pale flowers that bees work hard. A multi-stemmed one like this often begins when a tree is cut or broken and the stump sends up several shoots at once, though nobody has recorded what started this one.

No age or planting date is on record. If you know more about its history, tell us.

name: The Willow Oak of Steinway Street

location.address: 23-24 Steinway Street, Astoria

story:
In the words of NYC Parks, this oak's branches wave at the trains crossing the Hell Gate Bridge. It is a street tree, planted in the sidewalk in front of 23-24 Steinway Street in Astoria, and in 2024 Parks named it one of the Great Trees of New York City, calling it an extremely large willow oak on a busy commercial and residential stretch.

The trunk is 42 inches across, about three and a third metres round, which on a Queens sidewalk is a lot of tree. Willow oaks are oaks in everything but the leaf. Instead of the lobed oak leaf most people picture, they carry long, narrow, willow-like ones, so the crown reads soft and fine from below, and it still drops acorns. New York sits toward the northern end of the species' natural range, which runs mostly through the warmer Mid-Atlantic and South.

The bridge in that line is the Hell Gate railway arch over the East River, opened in 1917, and its approach viaduct crosses this part of Astoria above the streets.

A tree like this is the reason to walk a block you would otherwise drive through. Nobody has published its age or when it was planted. If you live on Steinway Street and know its story, tell us.

name: The River Birch of Corporal Kennedy Street

location.address: 35-26 Corporal Kennedy Street, Bayside

story:
Birches are not supposed to get this big on a sidewalk. NYC Parks said as much when it named this river birch one of the Great Trees of New York City in 2024. Its listing describes a very large multi-stemmed tree, an unusual size for a street tree, whose canopy arches right across Corporal Kennedy Street in Bayside.

The measurement needs one word of explanation. Parks gives 57 inches across, but that is the combined mass of several stems rising together, not one trunk. It is still a lot of birch. River birch is a native of stream banks in the eastern United States, usually planted in cities for its peeling, papery bark in shades of cream and cinnamon, and most of them stay modest. This one did not.

What a passer-by sees is a cluster of stems on the sidewalk outside number 35-26 and a crown that arches over the roadway to the other side. The latest public record of it dates from August 2024, so if you walk past and it looks in trouble, tell us.

Nobody has published its age or when it went in. If you know, that is worth hearing too. Bayside's railway station is a few minutes' walk away.

name: The London Plane of Alice Austen Park

location.address: Alice Austen Park, meadow south of the Alice Austen House, Rosebank

story:
Lightning hit this plane tree and it kept going. NYC Parks records the scar and the survival in the same breath, on a tree it believes was already growing around 1840, when John Austen bought the house on this shore of Staten Island and enlarged it.

John Austen was the grandfather of Alice Austen, who grew up in that house and became one of America's early women photographers, recording the Narrows, the harbour and the people around her for decades. If the Parks date is right, the plane in the meadow south of her house was part of the view she grew up with. Parks says only that it is believed, so read 1840 as a family-era estimate rather than a planting record.

The tree has the measurements to match a long life. Its trunk is 54 inches across, about four and a third metres round, it stands about 61 feet tall, and its crown spreads close to 60 feet over the grass. It was named one of the first Great Trees of New York City in 1985.

The park around it is open daily and free. The house itself, now a museum, keeps its own hours. Nobody has published a firmer date than the Parks estimate. If you know one, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad crown, spreading close to 60 feet, and a trunk 54 inches across marked by a lightning scar. It stands in the meadow south of the Alice Austen House.

name: The Empress Tree of Snug Harbor

location.address: Snug Harbor Cultural Center, west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse, Chapel Road, 1000 Richmond Terrace (Parks lists 914)

story:
Empress trees are built for speed, not endurance, which makes this one an outlier. When NYC Parks measured it for the first Great Trees list in 1985, its trunk was already 65 inches across, more than five metres round, on a species better known for racing up fast and coming apart young.

It stands on the west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse at Snug Harbor, the waterfront campus on Staten Island's north shore that was built in the nineteenth century as a home for retired sailors and is now a cultural centre. Parks puts its height at about 66 feet, 20 metres.

In spring it puts out upright clusters of purple, trumpet-shaped flowers before the leaves, and Parks notes that the leaves that follow can reach a foot across, big enough to make the tree look tropical in July. Both are worth seeing, but the flowers are the moment.

The grounds are free and open from dawn to dusk every day, though a few buildings and the Chinese Scholar's Garden charge a small fee. The address depends on whom you ask. Parks lists 914 Richmond Terrace, Snug Harbor uses 1000, and the playhouse is the landmark that settles it. No source gives an age or planting date. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge leaves, up to a foot across, and purple trumpet flowers in spring, on a trunk 65 inches across. It stands on the west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse.

name: The Willow Oak of Clove Lake

location.address: Clove Lakes Park, shore of Clove Lake, 150 ft north of Victory Blvd near the basketball courts

story:
Two oaks that look like willows stand on the edge of Clove Lake, and NYC Parks listed them together. When the city drew up its first Great Trees of New York City in 1985, this pair of willow oaks went on as a single entry, and the measured tree has a trunk 43 inches across, about three and a half metres round, and stands about 84 feet tall.

The setting suits them. Willow oaks are at home on damp ground, and these two grow right on the lake shore, about 150 feet north of Victory Boulevard near the basketball courts. Their leaves are long and narrow like a willow's, in a crown Parks measured at 43 feet across, but these are oaks all the same, and in autumn they drop small acorns.

Clove Lakes Park has another register tree. The tulip tree known as the Clove Lakes Colossus stands under two kilometres to the northwest, so the two make one lakeside walk.

Nobody has published the age of either oak or when they were planted. Parks names them as a pair without saying which is the bigger, so if you know the trees, or their story, tell us.

name: The Cedar of Lebanon of the Olmsted-Beil House

location.address: Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, Great Kills area

story:
Before he designed Central Park, Frederick Law Olmsted was a farmer on Staten Island, and this cedar stands on his farm. NYC Parks lists it as one of the trees remaining on the land Olmsted worked from 1848 to 1855, in the years before the park commission that made his name.

Parks does not say who planted it or when, and no second source does either. The cedar stands on Olmsted's ground, but what is documented of its link to the man himself stops at the property line. It was among the first trees named Great Trees of New York City, in 1985.

It is a big tree for a suburban lot. Parks gives a trunk 46 inches across, nearly three and three quarter metres round, a height of about 82 feet, 25 metres, and a crown about 40 feet wide. It stands 35 feet off the left front corner of the house, three feet from the driveway.

The house and grounds are a city park today. If you know when this cedar went in, and whether Olmsted had a hand in it, tell us.
